They routinely first blink or jerk their head to initiate the saccade. Although characteristic, impaired saccades are not peculiar to Huntington disease (see Chapter 12). Patients with schizophrenia, for example, also have abnormal saccades.

In addition, Huntington disease impairs ocular pursuit movements, which are the normal, relatively slow conjugate eye movements that follow (track) moving objects, such as a baseball thrown into the air or ducks flying across the horizon. Huntington disease patients typically show irregular, inaccurate, and slow pursuit movements. As with abnormal saccades, abnormal pursuit movements are not peculiar to Huntington disease. Notably, because both these ocular motility abnormalities are detectable in patients with schizophrenia, they also represent a physical expression of a psychiatric illness.

Even before dementia, which inevitably develops, patients with Huntington disease display inattentiveness, erratic behavior, apathy, personality changes, and impaired judgment. Dementia typically begins within 1 year of the chorea. Poor memory, impaired planning ability, and faulty judgment, especially in financial matters, characterize their dementia. In Huntington disease, as in Parkinson disease, the MoCA is more sensitive than the MMSE in detecting subtle cognitive impairment.

As almost an integral part of the disease, about 50% of patients have comorbid depressive symptoms that generally strike earlier rather than later in the illness. Most patients have agitation, anxiety, apathy, dysphoria, and irritability, and about 10% develop psychotic thinking. Sometimes, these symptoms precede both the dementia and chorea.

At a higher rate than in other neurodegenerative illnesses, up to 10% of individuals who are carriers or have overt signs of Huntington disease commit suicide. They tend to have had depression or anxiety, aggression, impaired judgment, or impetuous behavior—alone or in combination. They commit suicide most often before learning the results of their genetic testing or later when beginning to lose their independence. Notably, the suicide rate immediately before undergoing diagnostic testing exceeds that after receiving a positive result.

The caregiver stress involved with Huntington disease exceeds that with Alzheimer disease, especially because Huntington patients almost always have behavioral and cognitive impairments. Moreover, if the spouse of the Huntington patient has the role of caregiver, that person is also often the parent of one or more children with overt or presymptomatic disease.

Physicians can presumptively diagnose Huntington disease in a patient with chorea, dementia, and a relative with a similar disorder. Readily available DNA testing for patients and potential carriers, including a fetus, can confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

Reducing dopamine activity can suppress chorea. In the past, dopamine receptor-blocking antipsychotic agents were widely used, but due to their side effect profiles, current therapy centers upon medications that deplete dopamine from presynaptic neurons by inhibiting vesicular monoamine transporter-2 (VMAT2), a protein involved in dopamine storage and release (see Chapter 21). VMAT2 inhibitors include tetrabenazine (Xenazine), valbenazine (Ingrezza), and deutetrabenazine (Austedo). Nevertheless, despite their ability to suppress chorea, none of them improves other motor functions or reverses dementia. Moreover, because tetrabenazine depletes stores of norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and serotonin as well as dopamine, it sometimes also leads to sedation, depression, suicidal ideation and parkinsonism; the modified molecules deutetrabenazine and valbenazine are less likely to cause these adverse effects. In mild cases of anxiety, benzodiazepines may suffice. Fluoxetine may help with irritability, and there is some evidence that the depression may respond to TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs, and even olanzapine.

Sometimes symptoms appear in children and adolescents—individuals younger than 21 years of age. This variant, juvenile Huntington disease (also known as the Westphal variant of Huntington disease), comprises 10% of all cases and exhibits different manifestations from the more common adult form. Patients’ schoolwork declines and behavioral disturbances develop as the first signs. Also, rather than causing chorea as its initial physical symptom, juvenile Huntington disease presents with rigidity, dystonia, and akinesia (Fig. 18.19). Many affected children and adolescents look as though they have Parkinson disease. Another difference is that, unlike the adult variety, juvenile Huntington disease causes seizures. More importantly, juvenile Huntington disease progresses much more quickly and leads to death twice as rapidly as the adult form.

Huntington disease is the classic example of an illness transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern. The DNA abnormality underlying juvenile and adult varieties of Huntington disease—as with myotonic dystrophy, several spinocerebellar ataxias, fragile X syndrome, and other disorders—is a genetic mutation consisting of excessive trinucleotide repeats (see Chapter 6 and Appendix 2). The huntingtin gene, located on the short arm of chromosome 4, normally consists of 11–35 repeats of the trinucleotide cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG). Individuals with 36–39 repeats of this trinucleotide, a range neurologists classify as “indeterminate,” have no clinical signs of Huntington disease or merely a forme fruste of the disease; however, because the huntingtin gene’s tendency to enlarge from one generation to the next (see later), their children may have unequivocal disease. Individuals with 40 or more trinucleotide repeats invariably develop all manifestations of the illness. In general, with higher numbers of trinucleotide repeats the disease shows itself at a younger age and pursues a more rapid course. When the mutation consists of 60 or more trinucleotide repeats, the juvenile variant develops.

As with other genes containing expanded trinucleotide sequences, the huntingtin gene is unstable and tends to increase further in length in successive generations. The progressive expansion of the gene (amplification) explains why carriers of the mutation show signs at progressively younger ages in successive generations (anticipation). In addition, trinucleotide sequences enlarge further in sperm than in eggs. Thus, there is a preponderance of affected fathers among children with the disease; moreover, paternal inheritance confers a greater likelihood of an earlier onset and greater severity of the disease.

In Huntington disease, the excess of CAG repeats leads to an increased number of glutamine amino acids in the cytoplasmic protein huntingtin, which in turn causes degeneration of neurons containing this protein. Thus, neurologists designate Huntington disease and other illnesses transmitted by excessive CAG repeats as polyglutamine diseases. At the molecular level, glutamate and other excitatory amino acids overstimulate N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors. This pathologic excitotoxicity allows a fatal influx of calcium into neurons (see Chapter 21) that leads to cell death via apoptosis.

Apoptosis, the cell death that occurs in Huntington disease, ALS, and several other neurodegenerative illnesses, differs from necrosis, the common cell death that occurs in strokes, trauma, and tumors. Apoptosis is programmed, sequential, and energy-requiring. It often occurs as a normal, vital process. For example, apoptosis characterizes the cell death that allows for closure of the patent ductus arteriosus and involution of the thymus. On a histologic level, apoptosis does not provoke inflammation. For example, macrophages and other mononuclear cells do not infiltrate the area of cells dying of apoptosis. Neurologists regard apoptosis as orderly, regulated, and often purposeful cell death, but necrosis as unpredictable, bloody, and messy cell death.

Pathologically, Huntington disease causes degeneration through apoptosis of the striatal medium spiny neurons that produce GABA. The caudate, which is part of the striatum, shows pronounced atrophy, and its GABA concentrations fall to less than 50% of normal.

Atrophy of the caudate nuclei, almost a pathognomonic macroscopic finding, correlates roughly with the severity of dementia. The atrophy of the caudate nuclei permits the lateral ventricles to balloon outward; that is, develop a convex outline, giving rise to the description “bat-wing ventricles.” CT and MRI readily show the caudate atrophy and enlarged, convex ventricles (see Fig. 20.5 from Chapter 20). As Huntington disease progresses, the cerebral cortex also undergoes atrophy. PET studies demonstrate caudate hypometabolism even early in the illness.

By way of contrast, normal aging and Alzheimer disease cause primarily cerebral atrophy, without prominent atrophy of the caudate nuclei. In these non-Huntington conditions, the caudate nuclei still bulge normally into the lateral ventricles. The ventricles enlarge, but they maintain a concave contour (see Figs. 20.1, 20.3, and 20.18 from Chapter 20).

Sydenham chorea, originally known as St. Vitus’ dance, is one of the complications of—and major diagnostic criteria for—rheumatic fever. Sydenham chorea predominantly affects children between the ages of 5 and 15 years, and girls older than 10 years twice as frequently as boys. Although rheumatic fever has classically accounted for almost all cases of acute chorea in childhood, recently chorea-like movements have been found in children as a symptom of autoimmune or paraneoplastic encephalitis (see later and Chapter 19).

In the most plausible explanation of Sydenham chorea, group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, the cause of rheumatic fever, inadvertently trigger an antibody-mediated attack on the basal ganglia. The chorea usually coincides with rheumatic fever, but it may begin as long as 2–6 months afterward, when children have apparently recovered from their infection. The chorea lasts an average of 2 months but often reappears during recurrences of rheumatic fever. With the decreasing incidence of rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea seems restricted to small outbreaks—“mini-epidemics”—occurring mostly in neighborhoods with cramped living space and limited access to health care. Often, siblings and friends develop the disorder simultaneously or in quick succession. Neurologists often measure antistreptolysin O titers. Positive results confirm a recent streptococcal infection, but false-negative results are common.

The chorea begins insidiously with grimaces and limb movements (Fig. 18.20). Sometimes the movements make the child seem willfully hyperactive. Sydenham chorea is one of the most common neurologic causes of hyperactivity in children. A list of those causes would also include attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), side effects from medications or illicit drugs, Tourette syndrome and other tics, and withdrawal-emergent syndrome (see later).

The chorea’s significance lies not only in its warning of an underlying life-threatening condition (ruling out carditis is imperative!), but also because of its neuropsychiatric comorbidities. Obsessive-compulsive behavior, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and ADHD occur severalfold more frequently in children with Sydenham chorea compared to healthy controls. In addition, psychiatrists sometimes hold up Sydenham chorea along with Tourette syndrome as examples of pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS), but neurologists remain dubious about this concept (see later).

Some children reportedly also have learning disabilities following Sydenham chorea, but a causative role has not been proven. In any case, despite the serious nature of the illness, Sydenham chorea does not lead to frank cognitive impairment.

The chorea usually spontaneously resolves, but if it causes discomfort, functional impairment, sleeplessness, or exhaustion, neurologists prescribe a short course of either valproate or a dopamine receptor-blocking agent. In some cases, neurologists have sought to interrupt the inflammatory process and reduce the symptoms by administering steroids or intravenous immunoglobulins.

Oral contraceptive-induced chorea occasionally complicates use of oral estrogen-containing contraceptives. This variety of chorea, which is not associated with mental abnormalities other than anxiety, develops in young women several months after starting these contraceptives and resolves after stopping them.

Chorea gravidarum, a related disorder, develops almost exclusively in young primigravidas in the first two trimesters of their pregnancy. Emotional lability, delirium, and, rarely, psychotic thinking are comorbid with the chorea. The chorea may cause so much exhaustion that a spontaneous abortion occurs. To relieve severe chorea, women sometimes must undergo a therapeutic abortion. Once she delivers or the pregnancy is terminated, her symptoms resolve.

Many women affected by oral contraceptive-induced chorea or chorea gravidarum have had previous episodes of either condition or Sydenham chorea. Also, their close relatives often have had one of these conditions. Nevertheless, if chorea develops in a woman who is pregnant or taking oral contraceptives, physicians must consider conditions in addition to the estrogen-related choreas, including Sydenham chorea, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome (see Chapter 11), hyperthyroidism, autoimmune/paraneoplastic encephalitis, and even Huntington disease.

Hemiballismus consists of intermittent, large-scale flinging movements of one side of the body. A patient often will attempt to camouflage involuntary movements by converting them into apparently purposeful ones. For example, if her arm were to fly upward, she might incorporate the movement into a gesture such as waving to someone or smoothing her hair. Sometimes patients mechanically suppress involuntary movements of a limb by pressing their trunk or unaffected limb against it.

The movements resemble chorea, except that they are unilateral, more proximal, and more forceful (Fig. 18.21). Ballismus sits at the end of the sequence of progressively larger and more irregular involuntary movements.

Classic papers associated hemiballismus with lesions in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, but contemporary studies have found lesions in that area in less than one-third of cases. Another piece of evidence exonerating the subthalamic nucleus is that when neurosurgeons deliberately implant DBS electrodes in it, the damage rarely leads to postoperative hemiballismus or other movement disorders. Rather, lesions in the caudate nucleus or other basal ganglia may be responsible. In any case, because the causative lesion is small and situated nowhere near the cerebral cortex, patients with hemiballismus do not have comorbid cognitive impairment, seizures, or paresis.

Whatever the exact location of the lesion, the most common etiology is an occlusion of one or more of the small perforating branches of the middle cerebral artery that perfuse the basal ganglia. Similarly, vasculitis can affect those arteries. In individuals infected with HIV, toxoplasmosis lesions tend to develop in the basal ganglia and produce hemiballismus (see 20.11 from Chapter 20).

Most cases of hemiballismus resolve spontaneously, which is fortunate because neurologists have few treatments to offer. In cases that persist, dopamine receptor-blocking agents or dopamine-depleting agents may suppress the movements. Neurosurgeons have implanted DBS or ablated basal ganglia nuclei to relieve the movements, but they have had varying degrees of success.

The insidious development of psychiatric disturbances, cognitive impairment, and a variety of involuntary movements in adolescents or young adults characterizes Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). Because early diagnosis and treatment can reverse its manifestations, neurologists consider Wilson disease in the differential diagnosis of dementia or parkinsonism in children, adolescents, and young adults (see Box 7.3 from Chapter 7).

Wilson disease is transmitted via autosomal recessive inheritance. It results from a mutation in a gene carried on chromosome 13, which codes for a protein necessary for copper transport. The mutation leads to insufficient serum copper-binding and hepatic excretion. The resulting surplus of unbound serum copper, in turn, leads to destructive copper deposition in the brain, liver, cornea, and other organs. As its formal name implies, the illness primarily causes destruction of the liver and lenticular nuclei of the basal ganglia (see Fig. 18.1A).

Symptoms usually first appear during the late teenage years. The psychiatric symptoms, which may emerge before the physical neurologic signs, initially consist of disturbances in personality, conduct, and mood. With further deterioration, patients develop thought disorder and then cognitive impairment. When the deterioration culminates in dementia, Wilson disease would fall under the DSM-5-TR label of Major Neurocognitive Disorder due to Another Medical Condition. Especially in young adults, physicians may be misled toward a diagnosis of schizophrenia.

The neurologic signs are dysarthria, dysphagia, gait impairment, anosmia, and those reflecting basal ganglia damage: rigidity, akinesia, dystonia, nonspecific tremor, and the characteristic wing-beating tremor (Fig. 18.22). These movements tend to occur in combination and may be accompanied by corticospinal or corticobulbar tract signs.

Especially in adolescents, nonneurologic manifestations often overshadow neurologic ones. For example, liver involvement leads to cirrhosis, which is sometimes so severe that it causes hepatic encephalopathy and then liver failure. Deposits of copper in the cornea produce the signature Kayser–Fleischer ring (Fig. 18.23). It is detectable in almost 100% of patients when Wilson disease affects the brain, but in about 70% of cases if the disease affects only the liver. When present, the ring’s size and density correlate with the duration of the disease. With successful treatment of Wilson disease, the ring dissolves.

Despite the infrequent occurrence (1 per 30,000 persons) of Wilson disease, neurologists routinely test for it in adolescents and young adults who develop any of a variety of symptoms, including dysarthria, tremor, parkinsonism, dystonia, atypical psychosis, dementia, or cirrhosis. Because a Kayser–Fleischer corneal ring appears in almost all patients with Wilson disease who have neurologic manifestations, individuals suspected of having Wilson disease should undergo a slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist. They should also undergo determination of their serum ceruloplasmin (the serum copper-carrying protein) concentration, which in this illness is low to absent. Even when Wilson disease does not affect the brain, ceruloplasmin concentrations fall to low levels. Another test, though a more cumbersome one, is measurement of the 24 -hour urinary copper excretion; in Wilson disease, the absence of ceruloplasmin greatly increases urinary copper excretion. Genetic studies may confirm the diagnosis. MRI may help diagnose the illness, but characteristic changes often do not emerge until irreparable damage has occurred.

If physicians diagnose Wilson disease promptly, medical intervention will usually prevent progression and reverse some or all of the mental deterioration, abnormal movements, and nonneurologic manifestations, including Kayser–Fleischer rings. Patients should avoid copper-containing foods, which include many vegetables. Copper-chelating agents, such as penicillamine or trientine, and medications that block absorption of dietary copper, such as zinc, reduce the body’s copper burden. When the disease is refractory to medical treatment, liver transplantation can rescue the patient. Case reports describe improvement in dystonia with DBS of bilateral GPi in patients with Wilson disease, but this approach requires further investigation.

Neurologists use the term dystonia to describe involuntary movements due to sustained muscle contractions. Unlike other movement disorders, which result from unopposed contractions of a muscle group (such as chorea) or alternating contractions of agonist and antagonist muscle groups (tremor), dystonia results from the simultaneous contractions of agonist and antagonist muscle groups. Dystonia can involve one muscle group (focal dystonia) or many (generalized dystonia). In generalized dystonia, a patient’s limb (appendicular) muscles and neck, trunk, and pelvis (axial) muscles contract, causing prolonged twisting or turning (torsion), and forcing patients into unnatural, sometimes grotesque postures. Generalized dystonia often progresses over years to involve more and more regions until it encompasses the entire bodily musculature.

When dystonia is a manifestation of a known underlying condition, such as Wilson disease, neurologists refer to the movements as secondary dystonia. When the dystonic movements occur in isolation—without other neurologic abnormalities—neurologists refer to them as primary dystonia. Genetic traits contribute to primary and several secondary generalized dystonias (see later) more than to focal dystonias.

Primary dystonia, as previously noted, may cause physical incapacity but not dementia, although some studies have shown patients to have worse performance on neuropsychological testing. On the other hand, depending on the variety of dystonia and severity of disability, depression may be comorbid.

Dystonia, whatever its cause or area of involvement, usually has several unusual features. For example, “tricks” may suppress the movements. Skipping, walking backward, or dancing (with or without music) may overcome the gait abnormality. Similarly, lightly touching a twisted body part (a geste antagoniste; see later) may straighten it temporarily. In another unusual feature, dystonia tends to trigger compensatory movements that give patients a bizarre appearance. Probably more frequently than with any other involuntary movement disorder, physicians may misdiagnose dystonia as a functional disturbance because the movements are so unusual, idiosyncratic tricks override the movements, and the compensatory movements force patients into strange postures. Conversely, functional (psychogenic) movements can mimic dystonia (see later).

Early-onset primary dystonia or idiopathic torsion dystonia typically appears in 9- to 11 -year-old children, but almost always by the age of 26 years. It is most prevalent among Ashkenazi Jews due to a founder effect. The dystonia usually begins with torsion of one hand or foot (Fig. 18.24) and subsequently spreads to the other limbs, pelvis (tortipelvis), trunk, and neck (torticollis). Because muscles continually contract, they hypertrophy. Patients may lose their subcutaneous fat from the incessant exertion. Untreated, dystonia eventually incapacitates patients (Fig. 18.25).

A mutation in the DYT1 gene, located on chromosome 9, carries the illness in an autosomal dominant pattern, but its penetrance is only 30%. This mutation consists of a deletion of the trinucleotide GAG. Genetic testing can readily detect this mutation and establish the diagnosis. Several other genes also carry dystonia but vary as to whether they express the illness in a dominant or recessive pattern, which ethnic groups carry them, and their physical manifestations. Some authors have urged neurologists to order genetic testing, possibly exome-wide sequencing, for all patients with dystonia, even for those without a family history of any movement disorder. Routine tests—blood chemistry, MRI or CT, PET, and brain tissue analysis—reveal no consistent abnormality.

The mechanism through which the mutations produce the movements remains unknown. Several observations implicate a dopamine disturbance: levodopa alleviates dopa-responsive dystonia, and either prolonged or acute dopamine receptor blockade can cause dystonia (see later).

Anticholinergics, baclofen (Lioresal), and clonazepam (Klonopin)—a group neurologists have dubbed the “ABCs of dystonia treatment”—provide only modest and inconsistent benefit. However, DBS directed at the GPi greatly relieves dystonia, restores mobility, improves quality of life, and lifts mild-to-moderate depression. The benefit is often dramatic and lasts at least a decade. DBS usually permits reduction or elimination of oral medicines, often with improvement in mental status. Also, patients with dystonia who undergo DBS, unlike PD patients, do not exhibit postoperative cognitive changes. Children and adults are candidates. Carrying the DYT1 mutation and mildness of motor deficits preoperatively are predictors for a favorable outcome after DBS.

In a condition first described by Masaya Segawa and often named after him, dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD; DYT5) appears in children at an average age of 8 years. The dystonia follows a distinctive diurnal pattern: it is typically absent in the morning but becomes pronounced by the late afternoon and evening (Fig. 18.26). As with DYT1 dystonia, DRD first affects children’s legs, interfering with walking, and then progresses to become generalized. In DRD, parkinsonism or hyperreflexia may be concomitant with the dystonia.

The label “DRD” describes not only the diagnostic test for the illness, but also its treatment. Small levodopa doses, typically 300 mg/day or less, dramatically ameliorate DRD. Because of the success of levodopa in DRD, neurologists routinely give it as a therapeutic trial to a child who has developed dystonia or almost any movement disorder resembling dystonia. If the child improves, the neurologist can order genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis.

DRD exists in all ethnic groups. In affected families, cases usually appear in an autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance. Many different mutations of a gene carried on chromosome 14 impair the synthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin, which is a cofactor for both phenylalanine hydroxylase and tyrosine hydroxylase. The tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency, in turn, eventually leads to serotonin and dopamine deficiencies that become more pronounced over the course of a day as activities deplete their stores.

Several other neurologic illnesses—such as Wilson disease, juvenile Huntington disease, and many types of spinocerebellar degeneration—occasionally express themselves as generalized dystonia. Cerebral anoxia, stroke, encephalitis, brain tumors, and toxins also may be responsible. When an underlying condition causes the dystonia, neurologists designate it secondary or symptomatic dystonia.

One of these dystonia-producing illnesses, Lesch–Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive genetic disorder, produces one of neurology’s most bizarre symptoms: 2- to 13 -year-old boys (or, extraordinarily rarely, girls) develop ferocious self-mutilation (Fig. 18.27). In this quintessential neuropsychiatric abnormal behavior, children exhibit a compulsion for biting their own lips and fingers. This self-injurious behavior begins abruptly and furiously. In addition to the self-mutilation, they have intellectual disability, spasticity, seizures, and dystonia. By way of contrast, in intellectual disability accompanied by autism, self-injurious behavior usually consists of head banging and hitting that begins insidiously and remains relatively mild.

The basic abnormality in Lesch–Nyhan syndrome consists of a deficiency of an enzyme necessary for purine metabolism as the result of a mutation in the hypoxanthine phosphoribosyl transferase (HPRT1) gene. By late childhood, the mutation leads to an accumulation of uric acid in the blood (hyperuricemia) and renal insufficiency or failure. Although allopurinol corrects the hyperuricemia, it does not prevent the neurologic damage.

In recent years, physicians have increasingly recognized the wide variety of autoimmune neurologic syndromes—that is, disorders that result from autoantibodies that attack antigens in the nervous system. In retrospect, Sydenham chorea is an example of an autoimmune encephalitis.

Many cases of autoimmune encephalitis are associated with an underlying cancer, hence the term paraneoplastic. These syndromes consist of various movement disorders, often under the umbrella “dyskinesias,” seizures, confusion, and psychiatric disturbances (see Chapter 19). Dyskinesias or another of these symptoms may appear first or predominate. In the classic example, encephalitis associated with antibodies to the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor is associated with ovarian teratoma. In children, in contrast, autoimmune encephalitis is more often associated with a preceding herpes simplex encephalitis. The course typically begins with psychiatric and cognitive disturbances, followed in 1–2 weeks by dystonia or chorea in the face, limbs, and trunk. Its diagnosis relies on detection of antibodies to NMDA or other elements of the CNS in serum or CSF and a search for an underlying tumor or CNS infection. In most cases, removal of an underlying tumor, if present, and immunotherapies are effective.

In contrast to generalized dystonia, focal dystonias usually develop sporadically, occur 10 times more frequently than generalized dystonia, tend to arise in individuals in their fifth decade and older, and involve muscles in a single region of the body: most commonly the face or head (cranial dystonia), neck (cervical dystonia), or arm (brachial dystonia or writer’s cramp). Because focal dystonias recur in a particular pattern, neurologists refer to them as stereotyped. When only certain actions induce dystonia, neurologists call it task-specific. For example, writing, but not drawing or typing, may precipitate writer’s cramp (see later). Likewise, job-related motion may precipitate an occupational dystonia, and very frequent repetitive motion may underlie musician’s dystonia as occurs in proficient musicians who spend countless hours practicing. Nevertheless, as with primary generalized dystonia, patients’ cognitive capacity remains intact.

Rarely, focal dystonia relates to an identifiable cause, but more often, the etiology of focal dystonia remains unknown. Likely erroneously, in almost all cases, prior generations of neurologists and psychoanalysts, who previously were the same, attributed focal dystonias to subconscious conflicts. At another time, neurologists considered focal dystonias to be a form of tardive dyskinesia because the movements sometimes followed administration of dopamine receptor-blocking medications. However, while neuroleptics can cause focal tardive dystonia, most patients with focal dystonia have had no exposure to these medications and, aside from disturbances that the movements induce, they usually have no psychiatric issues. In most cases, dystonia relates to dysfunction of the central nervous system, but dystonia can also result from trauma and other forms of peripheral nervous system damage.

Injections of botulinum toxin into affected muscles may effectively, although temporarily, eliminate focal dystonia (Fig. 18.28). Botulinum toxin may also treat particularly troublesome isolated muscle groups in generalized dystonia or tardive dystonia. Botulinum toxin injections are approved for treating axillary hyperhidrosis (useful for patients with social anxiety disorder) and hypersalivation (such as that induced by neuroleptics). Physicians also inject botulinum toxins for cosmetic purposes to relax the facial muscles causing undesirable furrows (rhytides) of the forehead, eyebrow (“frown lines”), lateral canthus (“crow’s feet”), and other areas of the face and neck. Some researchers have reported that botulinum toxin injections into glabellar frown lines improves depressive symptoms, but further studies into this claim are needed.

In cervical dystonia, the most frequent form of focal dystonia, one or more neck muscles involuntarily contract to rotate or tilt the head and neck (Figs. 18.29 and 18.30). The resultant posture may consist of turning of the head to one side (torticollis), tilting to one side (laterocollis), flexion (anterocollis), or extension (retrocollis); most often these occur in complex combinations. The movements initially occur intermittently, but as the condition progresses, the abnormal postures become sustained, and a superimposed “dystonic tremor” often complicates the picture. Unlike other forms of dystonia, cervical dystonia usually causes pain because the muscle contractions forcefully compress and rotate the cervical vertebrae on each other, irritating the cervical nerve roots or facet joints.

Cervical dystonia most commonly represents primary dystonia, though rarely it can occur from structural lesions in the brain or cervical spine. Some cases are familial. In tardive dystonia due to long-term use of dopamine receptor-blocking agents, retrocollis often is prominent. Whatever the cause, intramuscular botulinum toxin injections reduce the movements as well as the pain. In severe cases, DBS has been helpful.

Blepharospasm, an easily recognizable and frequently occurring focal dystonia, consists of bilateral, simultaneous contractions of the orbicularis oculi (eyelid) and sometimes the frontalis (forehead) muscles (Fig. 18.31). The muscle spasms force the eyelids to close completely or partially, and cause disfiguring facial expressions. Although neurologists cannot establish the cause in most cases, various eye diseases, including “dry eye,” represent powerful risk factors. In contrast to eyelid tics, blepharospasm contractions are long, forceful, and not preceded by an urge.

To overcome the involuntary contractions, patients unconsciously learn tricks that temporarily suppress the contractions (Fig. 18.32). As with other focal dystonias, botulinum toxin injections usually reduce or abolish blepharospasm, at least on a temporary basis, with each set of injections.

Oromandibular dystonia consists of prominent contractions of the lower facial muscles and jaw muscles. Unlike the oral-buccal-lingual movements of tardive dyskinesia, the oral-buccal movements of oromandibular dystonia are symmetric, and tongue protrusion is usually absent.

When the contractions involve both the upper and lower face, causing both blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia, neurologists call the condition Meige syndrome (Fig. 18.33). This disorder mimics tardive dyskinesia except that, like oromandibular dystonia, it lacks tongue involvement. Neurosurgeons have performed DBS of the GPi to suppress the movements of Meige syndrome.

Spasmodic dysphonia consists of a distinctive speech abnormality caused by involuntary contraction of the laryngeal muscles when patients speak. In the most common type, the vocal cords adduct and lend the voice a strained tone—as if trying to speak while being strangled. Nevertheless, patients often can shout, sing, and whisper. Likewise, they can use the appropriate neighboring muscles normally to swallow and breathe. A less common variant causes abduction of the vocal cords with resulting breathiness of the voice.

Other cranial and cervical dystonias and head tremors often accompany spasmodic dysphonia. Clinical evaluation, often with laryngoscopy, can distinguish it from related conditions, such as essential tremor, vocal cord tumors, and pseudobulbar palsy (see Chapter 4). Electromyography-guided botulinum injections through the anterior of the throat directly into the laryngeal muscles reduce or eliminate involuntary contractions of the vocal folds and restore the voice.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Writer’s Cramp and Other Limb Dystonias
ce:section.ce:para: Limb dystonia usually involves the upper extremities more than the lower. When muscles contract involuntarily in individuals who use them repetitively as the basis of their livelihood, neurologists term the disorder occupational dystonia. The disorder prevents workers from doing their job. These dystonias are often task-specific, such that they emerge only with that particular action, while patients remain able to perform other functions with their affected hand.

In writer’s cramp, a clear example of an occupational dystonia, shortly after authors and others who use a pen or pencil begin to write, spasmodic contractions seize their finger and hand muscles. The contractions distort their hand and prevent it from properly holding the pen or pencil (Fig. 18.34). However, writer’s cramp is often highly task-specific and hence does not interfere with eating, buttoning clothing, or manipulating small objects—movements that require dexterity equal to handwriting.

Because affected individuals can still dictate or type material that they cannot write, writer’s cramp differs from the psychological phenomenon of writer’s block. Fatigue-induced cramps also differ from writer’s cramp in that they occur after hours of performing the same task, cause aching pain, and interfere with using the hand for any purpose.

Other examples include pianist’s, guitarist’s, and violinist’s cramps, in which repetitive, rapid, and intricate movements of these musicians’ hands and fingers precipitate cramplike movements. Similarly, brass and woodwind players are vulnerable to embouchure dystonia, in which playing their instrument triggers debilitating lip, jaw, and tongue muscle contractions. Focal occupational dystonias strike professional musicians as frequently as 1/200, which is greater than in any other professional group, and signal the end of high-level performances. Occupational dystonias also affect other workers who must repetitively perform a certain task, such as bricklaying and sewing.

Essential tremor consists of rhythmic oscillations (6- to 9- Hz) in one plane. It most often involves the arms, head, and voice. When tremor involves the arms or legs, it is usually, but not always, symmetric. Performing particular actions or holding the arms in certain postures elicits or accentuates the limb tremor (Fig. 18.35). Tremors of the head frequently conform to a “yes-yes” or “no-no” pattern.

Essential tremor usually appears in young and middle-aged adults. In many cases, it follows autosomal dominant inheritance but with variable penetrance. The pathophysiology underlying essential tremor is unclear. Some researchers have found reduced density of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum of patients with essential tremor, but not all studies have replicated this finding.

About 50% of affected individuals find that drinking alcohol-containing beverages suppresses their tremor. In almost all patients with tremor, as with many other neurologic conditions, anxiety precipitates or intensifies the movements. When anxiety affects the tremor, it increases the tremor’s amplitude but not its frequency.

Nonpharmacologic treatments may suffice for mild cases. Patients may benefit from wearing weights on their wrists, using capped mugs and a straw for drinking, and writing with thick rubber-covered pens. For safety, they should use electric shavers.

None of the pharmacologic treatments available is completely effective. However, β-adrenergic blockers, such as propranolol (Inderal), can help many cases of essential tremor and usually at doses that do not cause depression. The beneficial effect of these medicines supports the hypothesis that excessive β-adrenergic activity causes or exacerbates essential tremor. Primidone (Mysoline), an antiepileptic drug closely related to phenobarbital, alone or in combination with propranolol, also is effective in reducing the tremor, as is topiramate (Topamax). Medicines with less efficacy include benzodiazepines and other β-blockers. Botulinum toxin injections may be helpful for isolated head tremor.

For cases refractory to oral medications, DBS directed at the ventral intermedius (VIM) nucleus of the thalamus dramatically suppresses the tremor. To minimize risk, neurosurgeons can reduce operative time and likelihood of infection by implanting the electrodes unilaterally to improve the dominant hand. If successful, they can implant the electrodes contralaterally in a second procedure. While seemingly highly invasive for a relatively benign condition, DBS carries little risk, though long-term studies suggest that efficacy may wane over years. Neurosurgeons also use other methods for targeting and lesioning the VIM nucleus, including focused ultrasound and gamma knife therapy.

Recent studies show an association between essential tremor and cognitive impairment. One high-quality study showed a prevalence of 19% for dementia and 27% for mild cognitive impairment in patients with essential tremor. Clinicians need to weigh the risk of cognitive side effects when choosing medications to treat tremor.

Other fine, rapid tremors, because they also respond to β-blockers, probably originate in excessive adrenergic system activity. In contrast to the tremor of Parkinson disease, which characteristically occurs at rest and has a “pill rolling” appearance (see Fig. 18.8), these tremor types are more prominent with action and consist of a simple flexion-extension movement. They may represent a physical manifestation of anxiety, as in stage fright (performance anxiety), or the DSM-5-TR diagnosis Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia). Hyperthyroidism and other medical illnesses also cause tremor. Caffeine, the world’s most popular drug, and other stimulants induce tremors. Also, tremors are often medication-induced; common offenders include corticosteroids, the antiarrhythmic drug amiodarone, β-adrenergic agonists (such as those inhaled as bronchodilators), levothyroxine, and psychotropics including amitriptyline, lithium, valproate, SSRIs, and dopamine-blocking antipsychotics. Lithium and valproate regularly induce tremor even at therapeutic concentrations. Thus, a tremor in a patient with bipolar disorder who is taking lithium does not mean the lithium has risen to toxic levels or that the psychiatrist should decrease the dose of lithium. Tremor also can be a symptom of withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, opiates, or many other substances.

Cerebellar dysfunction causes a coarse, irregular tremor elicited by movement (see 2.11 from Chapter 2). The tremor of Wilson disease classically is described as “wing-beating” (see Fig. 18.22), but also can resemble the tremor of PD, cerebellar disease, or essential tremor. Because of its highly variable pattern, and possible responsiveness to treatment, physicians should always consider Wilson disease in young adults who develop a tremor. The fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome, which appears in older adults, includes intellectual disability, depression, anxiety, and agitation as well as tremor (see Chapter 13).

Palatal tremor, until recently called palatal myoclonus, consists of uninterrupted, symmetric, rhythmic contractions of the soft palate. The frequency—approximately 2 Hz—is consistent from patient to patient. It persists during sleep or coma. Most cases are caused by small brainstem infarctions that involve the medulla’s inferior olivary nucleus or its connections.

Tics consist of sudden, rapid, recurrent, and nonrhythmic movements. Neurologists classify them as simple or complex, and as motor or vocal (phonic). Simple motor tics include head tossing, prolonged eye blinking, shoulder jerking, and grimacing. Simple vocal tics consist of short, inarticulate sounds, such as throat clearing, grunting, and sniffing. The distinction between these two simple tics, however, is artificial because many vocal tics are simply the audible manifestation of motor tics of the larynx, pharynx, or thoracic diaphragm. For example, tics of the diaphragm forcefully withdraw air through the nose, causing sniffles.

Complex motor tics consist of coordinated actions of several muscle groups, such as jumping, stomping, skipping, and mimicking movements (echopraxia). Complex vocal tics range from words to phrases and include repeated words (echolalia) and obscenities (coprolalia; see later).

Tics often occur in bursts that persist for several seconds, vary, and recur. Over periods of weeks, months, or years, tics develop and subside. Tics may occur during sleep. Except for anxiety, no factor consistently exacerbates them. Using intense concentration and learned strategies, individuals can temporarily suppress tics.

Another feature is that a premonitory sensation—commonly perceived as a compulsion or irresistible urge—seems to provoke or at least precede tics in most patients. Patients gain relief if they allow tics to emerge, but suffer anxiety and an unpleasant intensification of the sensation if they do not. While characteristic of tics, a similar sensation precedes the movements in akathisia and RLS.

Simple motor tics develop at least briefly in as many as 30% of school-aged children, but by the end of adolescence almost all experience a spontaneous, complete remission. A disproportionate number of children with tics have a close relative with one or more tics. When their parents or siblings have tics, children are not only more apt to develop tics but also to develop them at a young age.

When adults display tics, they usually have either the persistence of a childhood-onset disorder or, after a quiescent period, the reemergence of one. Psychiatric comorbidities in childhood and a family history of psychiatric disorder constitute risk factors for persistence of childhood tics into adulthood. Compared to motor tics in children, which usually involve the head primarily, those in adults typically involve the neck and entire trunk. As individuals age, tics move from cephalad to caudal structures, that is, move from head to toe. Also, tics in adults carry different comorbidities, including substance abuse (cocaine or similar psychoactive substances), mood disorders, and anxiety and depression.

For a diagnosis of Tourette Disorder, the DSM-5-TR requires both vocal and multiple motor tics (although not necessarily concurrently) for longer than 1 year, with onset before 18 years of age (Fig. 18.36). Neurologists, who use similar criteria, tend to use the term Tourette syndrome.

Tourette syndrome affects boys more frequently than it does girls. This male preponderance also occurs in many other neurodevelopmental conditions, including dyslexia, stuttering, and autism. Tics appear on average at age 6–7 years, and in 90% of cases by age 13 years. When tics develop in childhood, there is usually a peripubertal exacerbation. In general, they relapse at the beginning of the school year and remit during the summer months. By their adult years, about 30% of affected individuals experience a complete remission and another 30% a substantial improvement.

At the onset of Tourette syndrome, tics usually involve only the face, eyes, and head, but in succeeding years tics spread caudally to affect the neck and shoulders, then arms and hands, and finally the trunk and legs. Because each tic may recede or replace another, Tourette syndrome varies from year to year in its repertoire, tempo, and intensity.

Vocal tics, an essential feature of Tourette syndrome, consist of irresistible, repetitive, stereotyped utterances—sounds, words, or, in the extreme, coprolalia. Vocal tics usually arise several years after the onset of motor tics and remain simple. They typically consist of only inarticulate sounds, such as sniffing, throat clearing, or clicks. However, many vocal tics rise to loud and disconcerting noises, such as grunting, snorting, or honking. Complex vocal tics consist of formed words that can culminate in unprovoked outbursts of obscene words, coprolalia. Although most coprolalia consists of only fragments of scatological words, such as “shi” or “fu,” some consist of strings of unequivocal obscenities. Related phenomena include intrusions of obscene thoughts (mental coprolalia) and involuntary obscene movements or gestures (copropraxia; Fig. 18.37).

When coprolalia complicates Tourette syndrome, it does not appear until about 6 years after the onset of motor tics. Usually coprolalia is merely socially reprehensible, but occasionally it can be dangerous, such as when a young Chinese girl’s vocal tic belittled Chairman Mao, or a Bronx teenager endlessly and uncontrollably repeated two words disparaging the New York Yankees, or a devoutly Catholic adolescent girl incessantly damned Jesus. Despite its dramatic and notorious aspects, physicians and the public have overemphasized coprolalia. It is not a diagnostic criterion for Tourette syndrome, and only about 20% of boys and 15% of girls exhibit it.

Psychiatric disturbances complicate Tourette syndrome in about 80% of cases and may dominate the clinical picture. The minority of patients who are unencumbered by psychiatric comorbidity experience relatively few behavioral disabilities and a better outcome. ADHD, the most frequently occurring comorbidity, affects about one-half of children with Tourette syndrome. It precedes the development of tics by 1–2 years.

A dilemma regarding hyperactive children with Tourette syndrome has centered on the concern that prescribing stimulants to control hyperactivity might worsen the tics. Studies have shown that although medical stimulants may cause a transient flare-up in tics, their benefits outweigh their risks in most cases.

Another common comorbidity of Tourette syndrome consists of obsessive-compulsive symptoms, either alone or as part of OCD. This comorbidity occurs in about 30% of both males and females, and, like ADHD, emerges several years after the onset of tics. Obsessions and compulsions in Tourette syndrome differ somewhat from those of pure OCD without comorbid Tourette syndrome. For example, obsessions in Tourette syndrome relate to sex, violence, and aggression, but those in pure OCD relate to dirt, germs, and illness. Similarly, compulsions in Tourette syndrome typically consist of checking and ordering, but those in pure OCD consist of more elaborate activities, such as handwashing or house cleaning.

Anxieties, phobias, and related disturbances also complicate Tourette syndrome in about 20% of patients of both genders. Their frequency and severity vary directly with the severity of the tics. Self-injurious behavior is estimated to affect 17%–35% of patients and is associated with complex motor tics, greater tic severity, and OCD. Severe tics can also cause direct injury such as when extreme neck movements result in myelopathy or radiculopathy.

Children with Tourette syndrome have normal intelligence and no propensity toward psychosis. Although many of them have learning disabilities, this problem may relate to the disorder only indirectly. For example, ADHD, social factors, and classroom disruptions would interfere with children’s education.

Many patients have soft neurologic signs and minor nonspecific EEG abnormalities. Their CT, MRI, functional MRI, PET, and diffusion imaging do not reveal consistent, specific abnormalities. However, some studies have found decreased volume of the caudate nucleus, and others have reported increased D2 receptor activity in the caudate. Tourette syndrome does not confer increased risk of epilepsy.

Genetic factors influence the risk of Tourette syndrome. For example, penetrance reaches almost 90% in monozygotic twins, and, depending on the criteria, 10%–15% of an affected individual’s first-degree relatives will have the disorder. In some cases, Tourette syndrome appears to be transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern, but no single causative gene has been identified.

Environmental factors are also likely to play a part in the etiology of Tourette syndrome. The theory of PANDAS (see earlier) proposes that, at least for a subset of patients, group A β-hemolytic streptococcus infections cause or trigger tics and Tourette syndrome (as in Sydenham chorea) and, more importantly, these infections induce obsessive-compulsive symptoms—all through antibody cross-reactivity or “molecular mimicry.” Despite its popularity, this theory lost traction after several clinical and basic science studies challenged it.

Evidence suggests that dopamine supersensitivity leads to the tics. For example, agents that reduce dopamine activity suppress tics, while dopamine-enhancing substances, like cocaine, exacerbate them. Other authors have reported that the severity of Tourette syndrome is associated with maternal smoking during pregnancy or with low birth weight, but these observations remain unconfirmed and speculative.

Current guidelines recommend that physicians consider comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics (CBIT) as initial treatment. CBIT comprises habit-reversal training, relaxation training, and a functional intervention to address situations that sustain or worsen tics. Studies had previously found that behavioral therapy, including “habit-reversal training,” reduced tics or at least postponed them to more socially acceptable times.

When tics require pharmacologic treatment, neurologists consider several approaches. Clonidine and guanfacine, α-adrenergic agonists, suppress tics through unknown mechanisms of action. Guanfacine may also help ADHD. A more potent treatment consists of reducing dopaminergic activity. For example, dopamine receptor antagonists, such as haloperidol, fluphenazine, and pimozide, suppress both vocal and most motor tics in about 80% of patients. Likewise, the dopamine depleter tetrabenazine lessens tics. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has indicated for use in Tourette syndrome not only the conventional dopamine receptor antagonists haloperidol and fluphenazine, but recently also aripiprazole. Putting aside withdrawal dyskinesias and other transient complications, dopamine receptor antagonist treatment of Tourette syndrome rarely causes tardive dyskinesia. In fact, one paper reporting an extremely low complication rate quipped, “Does Tourette syndrome prevent tardive dyskinesia?” Benefit from topiramate and from VMAT2 inhibitors has been reported, but the evidence is not strong.

Botulinum injections may temporarily eliminate bothersome, relatively focal motor tics. Several studies have shown DBS suppresses motor and vocal tics; however, they have not established the best target for electrode placement, and significant complications may occur. In addition, DBS directed at controlling tics will probably not improve the comorbid OCD. While some patients self-medicate with cannabis, studies have not established its value in treatment for tics.

A stereotypy consists of a repetitive, patterned, rhythmic, and often complex involuntary movement. Examples include slapping and flapping of the hands; twisting and wringing of the fingers; repetitive forceful closure of the jaw with grinding of the teeth (bruxism); and rocking, twirling, and weight shifting of the body.

Stereotypies may be manifestations of various conditions, including autism, Rett syndrome, Sydenham chorea, and Tourette syndrome. In individuals who are blind or have intellectual disability, stereotypies, such as continual rocking, appear to compensate for sensory deprivation. Similar repetitive behaviors also can appear during focal motor seizures—sometimes as their only outward manifestation. Cocaine use can cause 2–6 days of various repetitive movements, as well as tics, akathisialike leg movements (“crack-dancing”), and punding (see earlier). Despite their potential association with neurologic disorders, stereotypies can also be perfectly benign, occurring in perhaps 7% of neurologically normal children.

Myoclonus consists of generalized or focal, irregular, rapid jerks. It differs from most movement disorders in several respects. Myoclonus originates in abnormal discharges from motor neurons in the cerebral cortex, brainstem, or spinal cord rather than the basal ganglia. It may persist when patients are asleep or comatose. Also, unlike the spontaneous movements of chorea or Parkinson disease, myoclonic jerks can be triggered by voluntary movements or external stimuli, such as noise, touch, or light, in which case the myoclonus is labeled action- or stimulus-sensitive myoclonus.

Myoclonus is probably the most prominent physical manifestation of several illnesses psychiatrists are apt to encounter: serotonin syndrome (see Chapter 6), subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) (see Chapter 7), Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (see Chapter 7), cerebral anoxia, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, and autoimmune encephalitis (see earlier and Chapter 19). Myoclonus is also a common side effect of an elevated serum concentration of many medications, including gabapentin (Neurontin, Gralise, Horizant), pregabalin (Lyrica), penicillin, SSRIs and SNRIs, bismuth, and cyclosporine. For many of these agents, renal insufficiency increases the risk of myoclonus. In fact, uremia itself can lead to myoclonus.

When possible, remedying the underlying toxic-metabolic disturbance usually results in resolution of the myoclonus. Treatment with clonazepam, levetiracetam, or valproate may suppress myoclonus, but, of course, it does not affect the underlying disorder.

Psychiatrists may encounter myoclonus in their patients taking SSRIs, SNRIs, clozapine, or lithium. When myoclonus develops in patients taking an SSRI or SNRI, it suggests the serotonin syndrome (see Chapter 6). Physicians should avoid prescribing serotonergic agents in combination with medications that inhibit their metabolism, such as nonselective MAO inhibitors.

Not all myoclonus reflects pathology. Benign forms include hiccups, which are merely physiologic brief contractions of the diaphragm, and hypnagogic and hypnopompic jerks, which are the sudden, generalized muscle contractions that accompany the transitions into or out of sleep.

Hemifacial spasm, a type of focal myoclonus, consists of contractions of one or more muscles innervated by the facial nerve (the seventh cranial nerve) on one side (Fig. 18.38). In this disorder, spasms occur irregularly, often in flurries or clusters. Depending on their severity and anatomic distribution, spasms may disfigure the face and forcefully shut the eyelids. Like other types of myoclonus, hemifacial spasm routinely persists during sleep.

Hemifacial spasm often has an identifiable and correctable cause. In many cases, an aberrant blood vessel compresses and presumably irritates the facial nerve along its course distal to its exit from the pons. Sometimes, aberrant regeneration of the facial nerve after an injury, including Bell palsy, leads to the disorder.

Neurosurgeons can alleviate hemifacial spasm resulting from a compressing blood vessel by performing a microvascular decompression of the facial nerve. This procedure consists of inserting a cushion between the vessel and the facial nerve, similar to microvascular decompression of the fifth cranial nerve for treatment of trigeminal neuralgia (see Chapter 9).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Movement Disorders Due to Dopamine Receptor-Blocking Antipsychotic Agents and Other Medicines
ce:section.ce:para: As previously discussed, antipsychotic agents and other medicines that deplete dopamine from presynaptic neurons or block dopamine receptors potentially cause NMS (see Chapter 6), lower the seizure threshold, alter the EEG (see Chapter 10), and produce retinal abnormalities (see Chapter 12). They may also cause dramatic involuntary movements as well as parkinsonism.

When considering movement disorders induced by dopamine receptor-blocking agents, neurologists find it helpful to classify them as acute or tardive (late) based on the interval between initiating or increasing the dose of the medication and their onset. In this classification, acute movement disorders develop within days and tardive dyskinesias at 6 months or longer, but almost always within 12 months of starting the medication (Box 18.2b0015). Psychiatrists tend to use the term “extrapyramidal symptoms” to describe any involuntary movements due to these medications.

When they occur, acute movement disorders develop in about 50% of cases within the first 2 days and in about 90% of cases within the first 5 days of initiating or increasing the dose of the medication. First-generation neuroleptics cause these disorders more frequently than do newer antipsychotics. These disorders also result from use of dopamine receptor-blocking medications to treat nonpsychiatric conditions, such as metoclopramide (Reglan) as an antiemetic or antimigraine therapy.

Parenteral administration and combinations of offending agents are more likely to precipitate acute movement disorders. Other risk factors include youth, male gender, comorbid substance abuse, prior ECT, and preexisting brain damage. Cocaine abuse confers a 40-fold increased risk of developing acute dystonic reactions to antipsychotics.

Except for NMS, acute movement disorders usually spontaneously subside or respond to parenteral anticholinergics or antihistamines, but sometimes they persist indefinitely despite appropriate treatment.

Acute movement disorders fall into four categories: •
Acute dystonic reactions, including oculogyric crisis •
Akathisia •
Parkinsonism (see earlier) •
NMS (see Chapter 6)

Acute dystonic reactions consist of the abrupt development of limb or trunk dystonic postures, repetitive jaw and face muscle contractions, tongue protrusion, torticollis, or, in special cases, oculogyric crisis (Fig. 18.39). These may occur alone or in combinations, but in an oculogyric crisis facial, cervical, and/or jaw dystonia are frequently also present. Physicians must keep in mind that several serious neurologic disorders—seizures, tetanus, drugs of abuse, and strychnine poisoning—can cause similar movements. For example, patients who present with oculogyric crisis or other acute dystonia and do not respond to anticholinergics and antihistamines may be experiencing phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication.

The pathophysiology of acute dystonic reactions remains unknown. Of course, their temporal relationship to dopamine blockade suggests that lack of dopamine activity causes them. In the opposite scenario, because of the drug-induced blockade of dopamine receptors, a feedback loop may provoke an increased secretion of dopamine, or a dopamine-like neurotransmitter causes the movement. Another theory suggests that the movements’ favorable response to anticholinergics shows they result from absolute or relative excessive cholinergic activity.

In akathisia, nearly regular limb and trunk movements continually plague the patient (Fig. 18.40). Although akathisia can involve the trunk and arms, it predominantly affects the legs. It forces patients to move about and prohibits their sitting still or lying quietly in bed. When standing, patients tend to shuffle, march in place, or rock on their heels and toes. Although it predominantly affects the legs, akathisia can lead to repetitive semipurposeful movements of the arms, including scratching, hair smoothing, and rubbing. When sitting, which they find uncomfortable, patients squirm, sway back and forth, or rub their feet on the floor—hence the origin of the term “akathisia” (Greek, a, without + kathisis, sitting).

A subjective, integral component of akathisia—an irresistible need or compulsion to move—frequently disturbs the patient as much as the movements do. As with tics, a psychic urge compels movements; however, in akathisia, moving does not relieve the urge. For example, patients with akathisia may experience an insatiable restlessness or undeniable need to walk. Their distress sometimes forces them to abandon their medical regimen.

In subtle cases, akathisia often remains undetected because the movements are mostly an exaggeration of normal movements. Psychiatrists often need to distinguish akathisia from insufficiently treated anxiety, psychosis, or agitated depression to decide whether to decrease or increase the dose of an antipsychotic medicine for a restless patient with psychosis.

Akathisia may appear similar to movements induced by fluoxetine, cocaine (“crack dancing”), or excessive levodopa. In addition, although akathisia resembles RLS (see above and Chapter 17) and an urge to move their legs is characteristic of both conditions, akathisia patients do not experience the paresthesias that characterize RLS, and their movements are not specifically related to sleep. To emphasize that akathisia, tics, and RLS stem in part from uncomfortable sensations, one neurologist quipped that patients with these disorders move because they are distressed, but patients with most other movement disorders are distressed because they move.

The primary strategies for managing akathisia focus upon lowering the antipsychotic dose and avoiding use of multiple dopamine receptor-blocking agents. One meta-analysis of 10 different drugs found that vitamin B6, mirtazapine, and biperiden (an anticholinergic agent) were the most effective and best tolerated treatments for akathisia; propranolol (a β-blocker), trazodone, and mianserin were less desirable but also were better than placebo. Clonidine (an α2-agonist) was not included in that analysis but there is evidence that it may be beneficial.

Some physicians use the term “tardive dyskinesia” in a narrow sense to refer to the oral-buccal-lingual (also called choreic or orofacial) dyskinesia commonly induced by antipsychotics, which consists of stereotyped tongue, jaw, and face movements (Fig. 18.41). Others employ the term “tardive dyskinesia” more broadly by applying it to all types of abnormal movements due to dopamine receptor-blocking agents (see Box 18.2), and reserve the specific label “classic tardive dyskinesias” to denote the oral-buccal-lingual movements.

Clinicians can use the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) to describe the presence, locations, and severity of abnormal movements (Fig. 18.42). This instrument provides a global rating scale that allows physicians to assess pretreatment status and subsequent changes. However, even assuming interrater reliability, the AIMS has several drawbacks. It does not capture the fact that movements may vary in intensity over time. The rating of severity from 1 to 5 is subjective and coarse. The AIMS does not recognize akinesia or hypokinesia, which should carry as much diagnostic weight as dyskinesia. It lacks nuance in failing to distinguish among chorea, dystonia, tics, and stereotypies. Finally, it omits several important movements, such as tremor, dysarthria, and respiratory tics.

Most, but not all, studies have concluded that the overall incidence of tardive dyskinesia is higher with first-generation than second-generation antipsychotics. Explanations for that finding include the observations that dopamine receptor-blocking antipsychotic agents with a high affinity for D2 receptors, which are mostly the first-generation neuroleptics, remain the strongest risk factor for tardive dyskinesia; second-generation antipsychotics act primarily on 5HT2A receptors and produce a high 5HT2A/D2 blockade ratio; second-generation antipsychotics adhere either weakly or transiently to the D2 receptor; and some, such as aripiprazole, partially agonize as well as block the D2 receptor. Quetiapine and clozapine, which have negligible affinity for dopamine receptors, are not associated with tardive dyskinesia. Other powerful risk factors include the duration of treatment and total medication dosage, age greater than 60 years, and female gender (especially for patients older than 65 years). Interesting but less powerful risk factors include prior history of medication-induced extrapyramidal side effects, dementia or other sign of brain damage, underlying affective rather than psychotic illness, and certain genes.

Some studies have found that the yearly incidence of tardive dyskinesia remained constant throughout medication exposure and concluded that patients have the same chance of developing this complication during the first year as during the fifth year of treatment. Others have reported that the incidence increases slightly with longer duration of treatment.

Despite its limitations, the classic dopamine receptor supersensitivity theory remains consistent with several of the condition’s major clinical features (Fig. 18.43). Tardive dyskinesia begins 6 months or more after the initiation of dopamine receptor-blocking medicines. Changes that expose the postsynaptic neuron to increased dopamine activity—reducing the dosage of the dopamine receptor blocker, stopping it, or adding levodopa—intensify the movements. Likewise, increasing the medication dosage, which reduces dopamine activity, suppresses the movements. The traditional theory views tardive dyskinesia as the result of upregulation of D2 receptors, but evidence from a monkey model has suggested that it is D3 receptors rather than D2 receptors that become supersensitive.

An alternate theory attributes the disorder to deficient or abnormal GABA activity in the striatum. Another posits that the glutamate system triggers excitotoxicity through NMDA receptors. Still another suggests that catecholamine metabolism creates neurotoxic free radicals. A combination of mechanisms likely contributes to the development of tardive dyskinesia.

The best treatment is prevention. To the extent possible, physicians should avoid prescribing antipsychotics and other medications associated with tardive dyskinesias. When their use is warranted, physicians should prescribe minimal doses. Once tardive dyskinesia appears, physicians should resist a natural temptation to abruptly stop the medicine. They should taper it—over weeks or months—because abruptly stopping it may unmask the withdrawal-emergent syndrome (see later).

Alternatively, switching from a first- to a second-generation antipsychotic or from one second-generation agent to another sometimes helps. Although the benefit may take months to materialize, switching to clozapine in cases of refractory, disabling tardive dyskinesia often is an effective strategy. Patients on clozapine need to be monitored for agranulocytosis, but as of February 2025 the FDA no longer requires participation in the risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS) program for clozapine or reporting results of absolute neutrophil count (ANC) blood tests for patients to obtain it.

VMAT2 inhibitors—tetrabenazine (off-label at this time), valbenazine, and deutetrabenazine—reduce tardive dyskinesias by depleting dopamine from presynaptic neurons (see 21.2 from Chapter 21). However, depression, suicidal ideation, parkinsonism, and possibly NMS may complicate their use, though risk is higher for tetrabenazine than for the others. As a last resort, the physician can reduce dopamine activity by restarting or increasing the dosage of a typical dopamine-blocking medication or substituting a more potent one. However, this strategy risks creating a vicious cycle where recurrence of the dyskinesia requires additional medication.

A different approach advocates counterbalancing the enhanced dopamine activity by increasing ACh activity (see Fig. 18.11). Despite the theory’s plausibility, physostigmine, which prolongs ACh activity, and ACh precursors, such as deanol (Deaner), lecithin, or choline, confer only brief benefit. Rigorous studies of a possible role for the anticholinesterase medications approved for Alzheimer disease—donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine—to treat tardive dyskinesia are lacking. The opposite approach, giving anticholinergics, also does not help.

Medications that affect other neurotransmitters also fail to help. For example, GABA agonists such as baclofen, calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem (Cardizem), lithium, and opiates provide no consistent relief. Medications with some evidence of benefit are benzodiazepines and vitamin E, but the effects are mild.

Neurologists hesitate to use botulinum injections for tongue dyskinesias. Their concern is that injecting the tongue’s main muscles (the genioglossus and geniohyoid) would require a needle to pass through their rich vascular supply and risk an uncontrollable hemorrhage. Moreover, botulinum might weaken tongue or throat muscles enough to occlude the airway.

Preliminary studies found that DBS directed at the GPi ameliorates oral-buccal-lingual and other varieties of tardive dyskinesia. Moreover, DBS often permits patients to discontinue the medicines that were prescribed to reduce the movements. DBS causes no cognitive impairment or exacerbation of depression.

The American Academy of Neurology published a guideline in 2013 and an update in 2018 summarizing evidence-based recommendations regarding treatment of tardive syndromes. The strongest evidence supports deutetrabenazine and valbenazine as effective treatments. Clonazepam and ginkgo biloba extract—an antioxidant—are of probable benefit. The authors also deemed amantadine and tetrabenazine to be options, though evidence for their beneficial effect is weaker. DBS targeting the GPi was felt to be possibly effective but can be considered when movements are intractable. The publications examined many other interventions—including numerous medications and supplements and withdrawal or switching of neuroleptics—but found data to be insufficient to recommend any of them.
Pharmacotherapy for tardive dyskinesia may not be necessary. Even without intervention, approximately 33% of oral-buccal-lingual cases undergo remission spontaneously.

A variant of tardive dyskinesia, tardive dystonia, consists of sustained, powerful, twisting movements predominantly of the neck, upper arms, and trunk (Fig. 18.44). Retrocollis, reflecting contraction of the extensor neck muscles, is a common pattern. This movement is more typical of tardive dystonia than of primary cervical dystonia in which torticollis and laterocollis predominate. Oral-buccal-lingual dyskinesia, blepharospasm, or akathisia often accompany tardive dystonia. Overall, tardive dystonia resembles the dystonia of Wilson disease, juvenile Huntington disease, and DYT1 dystonia.

A relatively short exposure to dopamine-blocking agents, sometimes as brief as 3 months, can cause tardive dystonia. Thereafter, it complicates exposure at a low but constant yearly rate. Spontaneous remissions occur in about 12% of cases.

Several entirely different medicines may suppress tardive dystonia. In contrast to their lack of benefit in oral-buccal-lingual dyskinesia, anticholinergics often reduce tardive dystonia, as they do other forms of dystonia. Clozapine and VMAT2 inhibitors, which reduce dopamine activity through different mechanisms, often help. Botulinum injections may alleviate dystonia in severely involved specific muscle groups, such as the neck extensors.
DBS alleviates tardive dystonia just as it does DYT1 dystonia. It provides the same benefits and safety margin as when used for oral-buccal-lingual dyskinesia.

Tardive akathisia, which resembles the acute disorder, persists for longer than 6 months after the medication is begun. In addition, it may appear only after the patient has stopped the offending medication. As with tardive dystonia, other tardive dyskinesias often accompany tardive akathisia.

Opioids, benzodiazepines, and propranolol can sometimes alleviate tardive akathisia. Reported benefits from reserpine, tetrabenazine, amantadine, anticholinergics, and other medications remain unconfirmed.

Tardive tics, another variety of tardive dyskinesia, include vocal tics, which consist of persistent simple vocalizations, such as grunts, and respiratory tics, which consist of sudden, loud, irregular gasps. Tardive dyskinesias also include tardive tremors and other persistent movements. As in cases of tardive dystonia and akathisia, oral-buccal-lingual movements often accompany each of these varieties of tardive dyskinesia.

The rabbit syndrome—rapid, regular up-and-down or occasionally side-to-side jaw and lower mouth movements—sometimes follows prolonged use of antidepressants or first- or second-generation antipsychotics. To avoid confusion with oral-buccal-lingual dyskinesia, tongue or upper face movements preclude a diagnosis of rabbit syndrome. It also differs from that variety of tardive dyskinesia because it follows the use of psychotropics that do not block D2 receptors, and anticholinergics regularly suppress it.

Involuntary movements sometimes appear after abrupt cessation of prolonged treatment with dopamine-blocking agents. This condition, the withdrawal-emergent syndrome, usually consists of mild to moderately severe chorea with motor impersistence and restlessness. The explanation for the withdrawal-emergent syndrome—a variation of the one for tardive dyskinesias—is removal of a dopamine receptor-blocking medication that suddenly exposes supersensitive dopamine receptors to relatively high concentrations of dopamine.

The withdrawal-emergent syndrome typically affects children and lasts 4–12 weeks. Episodes longer than 6 months probably represent tardive dyskinesia. Intolerable withdrawal dyskinesias may force physicians to reinstitute the offending medication and then taper it more slowly.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Movement Disorders from Other Psychiatric Medications
ce:section.ce:para: SSRIs may cause hyperkinetic movement disorders, inducing myoclonus, tremor, bruxism (teeth grinding), or akathisia-like leg movements. As discussed previously, SSRIs may cause the serotonin syndrome (see also Chapter 6). Despite these caveats, serious adverse reactions to SSRIs occur in only a small proportion of patients—usually when SSRIs are administered in high doses, in combination with other medications (such as nonselective MAO inhibitors), or in patients with a preexisting neurologic disorder.

About 10% of patients taking TCAs develop a fine, rapid tremor that resembles essential tremor and responds to propranolol. The antidepressant amoxapine, which has dopamine antagonist properties, can induce parkinsonism; however, almost no other antidepressant causes parkinsonism or other signs of extrapyramidal dysfunction. Antidepressants also predispose patients to REM sleep behavior disorder (see Chapter 17). Some reports have found that bupropion (Wellbutrin and Zyban) can induce RLS, while in other cases it may improve that condition.

Lithium, even at therapeutic serum concentrations, can induce a tremor that resembles essential tremor. At toxic concentrations, it produces a severe, coarse intention tremor often accompanied by ataxia of the trunk, that is, signs of cerebellar dysfunction. Sometimes lithium causes signs of parkinsonism. Although adding propranolol may suppress a mild tremor, reducing the lithium dose is usually preferable.

Antiepileptic drugs often cause tremor, ataxia, and other movement disorders, but generally only at toxic serum concentrations. As an exception, valproate may cause a tremor independent of dose. Nonpsychiatric medications that commonly induce tremor include β-agonist bronchodilators, levothyroxine, amiodarone, corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants such as tacrolimus.

Physicians must pause before attributing every case of involuntary facial, tongue, and jaw movement to a complication of an antipsychotic. As already discussed, physicians might observe similar movements in Huntington disease, cranial dystonia, tics, and stereotypies.

Stereotyped movements of the face, mouth, or tongue appear sporadically in medication-naïve schizophrenic patients and were described before the introduction of antipsychotics.
